newsitem.title: USA: IPO VIEW-Vail a hot spot in percolating US IPO market.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW-Vail a hot spot in percolating US IPO market.

text.p: Vail Resorts Inc. is coming to Wall Street this week with near-perfect conditions for the tiny Colorado ski resort's initial public offering, along with a crop of other hot deals.

Vail plans to offer 10.5 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol "MTN" and stands to reap about $200 million. Shares are expected to cost between $19 and $21 each and IPO analysts are forecasting a lift of about 10 percent when the stock opens up for trading.

"Vail has got a lot of prestige and they generate a lot of cash per skier. They are using the money to cut indebtedness, which should make for a stronger company," said David Menlow of Springfield, N.J.-based IPO Financial Network.

On top of its image as the mountain where the rich and famous hit the slopes is the tantalizing prospect of consolidation. Acquisitions in the still largely-fragmented North American ski industry could benefit Vail, one of the industry's top dogs.

Kevin Eldrige, analyst at Vancouver-based Salman Partners, said acquisitions has been one of the key reasons behind the success of rival Canadian ski resort Intrawest Corp., which owns Blackcomb and Whister in Canada and Colorado's Copper Mountain.

Vail hit a snag earlier this year when its aggressive acquisition strategy in Colorado sparked antitrust concerns at the U.S. Justice Department. In addition to its flagship Vail resort, the company also owns owns ski resorts Beaver Creek, Keystone and Breckenridge. It agreed to sell another resort, Arapohoe, by June 2 as part of a settlement.

Improving market conditions could also drive the IPO. Money managers, flush with cash pouring into mutual funds, are looking towards the IPO market for better values compared to blue chip stocks, where prices have been pushed to new lofty peaks in the past few months.
"It's still too early to tell if this fairly robust week is a pattern but...the market's very strong and there are buyers," said Bruce Misset, head of the new issues operations of Oppenheimer & Co.

Other deals that institutional investors are clamoring for include China Eastern Airlines, Yurie Systems Inc., Ciena Corp. and Circuit City Stores Inc.'s CarMax chain of auto superstores. Analysts say these deals could rise even higher than Vail, fetching premiums of several points or more.

Last week, 23 companies went public raising $1.3 billion, according to MCM CorporateWatch. Three companies were able to charge higher-than-expected IPO prices and several deals posted very strong opening-day premiums.
It was the first sign of some strength percolating in the new issues market since a seasonal holiday slowdown.

"Without question, the tone has changed dramatically from the 1996 close-out, although the air of sensibility still prevails," said Menlow. "Underwriters still recognize they can't bring issues that don't have some level of fiscal seasoning."

One surprising undercurrent in last week's market that IPO analysts noted with surprise was the debut of medical malpractic insurer SCPIE Holdings Inc. and mortgage bank HomeSide Inc.. Both were priced below their estimated ranges, which is usually an indication of weak demand for a stock. Yet both deals had strong opening premiums.
